spans.text: H3’s connection migration remains robust, maintaining stable performance even in proxy-enhanced environments, ensuring seamless network transitions.
When the bandwidth reaches 1 Gbps, QUIC becomes 45.2% slower than HTTP/2.
The bitrate reduction goes up to 9.8%.

If a user walks out of their house and switches networks, the client simply continues sending UDP packets with the same CID, and the server processes them without a single millisecond of interruption.

Cloudflare’s edge logs ([publicly visible](https://blog.cloudflare.com/http-3-the-past-present-and-future/)) show that this is responsible for a measurable improvement in mobile hand-off latency for QUIC connections.

In a traditional HTTPS stack (TCP + TLS 1.3), establishing a secure connection requires two round-trips (RTTs): one for the TCP handshake and one for the TLS handshake. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 directly into its own transport handshake, reducing connection setup time to a single round-trip (1-RTT) or even 0-RTT for returning clients.

claims.text: QUIC connection migration maintains stable performance when mobile clients transition between networks—downloading 10 MB files in approximately 15 seconds even during simulated IP address changes with 4% packet loss and 50 ms latency present. This eliminates the need for TCP's requirement to reestablish connections and re-upload request state after a network change.

claims.text: Under severe conditions (4% packet loss, 50 ms latency), QUIC downloads a 10 MB file in 15 seconds versus HTTP/2's 106 seconds without proxy acceleration. Unlike HTTP/2, which requires congestion control algorithm selection (BBR versus NewReno) to achieve comparable speeds, QUIC's performance remains consistent regardless of congestion control choice—indicating the head-of-line blocking elimination is load-bearing in lossy conditions.

claims.text: QUIC's receiver-side processing overhead negates its head-of-line blocking advantages on high-speed networks. At 1 Gbps, QUIC is 45.2% slower than HTTP/2 on Chrome; on real 5G networks, QUIC reduces video streaming bitrate by up to 9.8% compared to HTTP/2. The bottleneck is not network delivery but kernel-to-userspace packet processing and user-space ACK generation—making QUIC slower precisely where bandwidth is abundant.

claims.text: QUIC's frame-level observability enables operators to log every congestion event to histograms and ship results to telemetry backends. Kernel TCP only offers passive tcp_probe telemetry, forcing operators to infer behavior from aggregate metrics. This direct observability lets teams iterate on congestion control in real time without rebooting.

claims.text: QUIC's connection migration uses an independent Connection ID that survives network changes, allowing clients to switch from LTE to WiFi without reconnecting. Cloudflare's field measurements show this produces measurable improvements in hand-off latency for production QUIC connections, whereas TCP's 4-tuple binding forces application reconnection logic.

claims.text: QUIC combines the TCP handshake and TLS handshake into a single round-trip (1-RTT) versus the traditional HTTP/2 stack requiring 2-RTT. On high-latency networks like satellite or intercontinental mobile links, this eliminates 50–100ms of setup delay before any data transfer begins, shifting the tradeoff calculation for connection architecture decisions.
